question:
Patient note:
A 95-year-old man who lives independently in a small studio apartment attached to his daughter’s home was dispatched to the hospital after the visiting volunteer who brings him lunch each day noticed that he was breathing a little faster than usual and appeared momentarily uncertain of the day of the week; she called emergency services when he twice paused to catch his breath while crossing the kitchen. According to the regional health-information exchange, his chronic problems are limited to well-controlled stage-1 hypertension managed with a low-dose thiazide diuretic and mild knee osteoarthritis treated only with as-needed acetaminophen; his last primary-care visit four months ago documented normal cognitive testing, a serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL, and no evidence of end-stage cardiac, hepatic, pulmonary, or renal disease. He has never undergone solid-organ transplantation, has never received chemotherapy or long-term corticosteroids, and denies any diagnosis that would require biologic immunomodulators. The paramedic narrative describes an alert, thin gentleman seated upright on the sofa, speaking in full sentences but pausing to take deeper breaths; fingertip saturation on room air read 88 %. A vented facemask connected to the ambulance blender was titrated to deliver 35 % inspired oxygen, resulting in a steady saturation of 92–93 %. No nebulizers, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors, analgesics, or antipyretics were administered during the nine-minute suburban transport, and the single 20-gauge antecubital catheter that was placed remained saline-locked on arrival. Upon stretcher entry to the intensive-care triage bay—and before any hospital-initiated therapy—the first complete set of observations was obtained: an oral temperature of 37.1 °C, a regular pulse of 90 beats per minute on the transport monitor, a respiratory rate counted over sixty seconds at 20 breaths per minute without nasal flaring or accessory-muscle recruitment, and a non-invasive blood pressure cycling consistently at 128/68 mm Hg on back-to-back cuffs. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic with brisk capillary refill; there was no peripheral cyanosis or mottling. Neck veins were flat at 30°, carotid upstrokes were sharp, and extremity pulses were palpable at 2+. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1, physiologic split S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds were diminished at the left base with late-inspiratory crackles, percussion there was dull, and tactile fremitus was slightly increased compared with the right; no wheeze or rhonchi were appreciated. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender; bowel sounds were present. There was no pedal edema, clubbing, or calf tenderness. Neurologically he opened his eyes promptly to voice, correctly stated his name and the city but was unsure of the exact date, and obeyed two-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14; speech was clear, pupils were equal and reactive, and strength was 5/5 throughout. Eight minutes after bay placement, while the mask continued to provide the same 35 % oxygen, a right radial arterial sample was analyzed, returning a pH of 7.40, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and a PaO₂ of 74 mm Hg; end-tidal capnography registered 37 mm Hg, suggesting adequate ventilatory matching. Simultaneous point-of-care chemistry revealed sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 106 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.2 mg/dL—nearly identical to his outpatient baseline, making an acute renal insult unlikely. A complete blood count from the same arterial stick demonstrated a white-cell concentration of 10 500 /mm³ with 74 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 36 %, hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, and platelets 242 000 /µL. Venous lactate measured at bedside was 1.6 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiography obtained before any antimicrobial or diuretic therapy showed a small consolidation in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe with trace pleural effusion and a normal cardiac silhouette. Focused cardiac ultrasound performed at the bedside revealed a vigorously contracting left ventricle, no regional wall-motion abnormality, and an inferior vena cava measuring 1.4 cm that collapsed more than 50 % with quiet inspiration, suggesting euvolemia rather than volume overload. A bladder scan indicated 110 mL of urine, and nursing reported that he had voided normally that morning. Twelve-lead electrocardiography printed during the arterial draw showed normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats per minute, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, QTc 420 ms, and no acute ischemic change. Up to the point the critical-care team assumed responsibility—approximately twenty minutes from front-door arrival—he had still received no intravenous crystalloid boluses, no antibiotics, no bronchodilators, no diuretics, and no vasoactive medications; oxygen via the 35 % mask remained the only therapy. Consequently, the contemporaneous physiologic and laboratory measurements—temperature 37.1 °C, systolic pressure 128 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 68 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats per minute, respirations 20 per minute, arterial pH 7.40, serum sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, hematocrit 36 %, white blood cell count 10 500 /mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 0.35, and arterial oxygen tension 74 mm Hg—accurately capture his untreated presentation for suspected left lower-lobe community-acquired pneumonia accompanied by mild hypoxemic respiratory compromise in the absence of underlying immunodeficiency or major organ failure.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology points, age points, and chronic health points. Using the supplied admission measurements:
- Temperature 37.1 °C = 0; mean arterial pressure (128 + 2 × 68)/3 = 88 mm Hg = 0; heart rate 90/min = 0; respiratory rate 20/min = 0.
- FiO₂ 0.35 is below 0.50, so score PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 74 mm Hg is above 70 = 0.
- Arterial pH 7.40 = 0; sodium 140 = 0; potassium 4.1 = 0; creatinine 1.2 mg/dL = 0; hematocrit 36% = 0; WBC 10,500/mm³ = 0.
- Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 14 = 1. Acute physiology subtotal = 1.
- Age 95 (≥75) = 6. No qualifying severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise = 0.
Sum: 1 + 6 + 0 = 7.
Final answer: 7
